t: Count Special Subsequences — Fraction Hashing on (p,q) vs (r,s)
o: Count index quadruples p < q < r < s with gaps > 1 and nums[p]*nums[r] == nums[q]*nums[s]. Rewriting as nums[p]/nums[q] == nums[s]/nums[r] decouples the problem: for each r, count pairs (p, q) with q <= r-2, p <= q-2 by their reduced fraction, and pairs (s, r) with s >= r+2 by the same reduced fraction; matching fractions multiply. Example 2's three quadruples all arise this way. The (p,q) counter grows incrementally as r advances, giving O(n^2) total.
k: The equation is equivalent to the reduced fraction nums[p]/nums[q] equaling nums[s]/nums[r], letting left and right sides be counted independently per r.
Valid (p,q) pairs for a given r are exactly those with q <= r-2 and p <= q-2, so the pair counter can be extended incrementally as r increases (add column q = r-2).

a.i: Check all index quadruples directly. O(n^4) is far too slow for n = 1000 but is the clearest specification of the problem and useful for stress-testing the fast solution.
s: Four nested loops p < q < r < s with the gap conditions.

a.i: Sweep r left to right. Before processing r, insert all pairs (p, q=r-2) with p <= q-2 into a global counter keyed by the reduced fraction (nums[p]/g, nums[q]/g). Build a fresh counter of reduced fractions (nums[s]/g, nums[r]/g) for s >= r+2 and add the dot product with the global counter. Each phase is O(n) per r, totaling O(n^2).
s: For r from 0 to n-1: if r >= 2, add pairs (p, q=r-2), p <= q-2, keyed by reduced (nums[p], nums[q]).
Build counter R over s >= r+2 keyed by reduced (nums[s], nums[r]).
Add Σ_key R[key] * L[key] to the answer.
a.t: O(n^2) — inserting O(r) pairs per r, building O(n-r) right entries per r, and an O(|R|) dot product per r sum to ~1.5e6 operations at n = 1000.
a.sp: O(n^2) — the global (p,q) counter can hold ~n^2/2 distinct fractions.

w: Present the fraction-decoupling insight prominently — it is what collapses O(n^4) to O(n^2). Pitfalls: the gap conditions translate to q <= r-2, p <= q-2, s >= r+2 (off-by-one here breaks everything); reduce fractions by GCD before hashing (values up to 1000 make a*1001+b a safe key); and the answer can exceed 32 bits (use 64-bit internally). Follow-up: what if the gap requirement were removed? Then plain product-bucket counting suffices; with gaps, the incremental-column trick is the crux.
